If you read 1984 by Orwell and you liked it, you will also like this game. This is a text-based surveillance-detective. You work for the government and investigate some bombing by syphoning through chunks of peoples data – emails, chats, phone calls, banking details, past interactions, interrogations etc. The game allows you to make some choices, so you can miss a bomb or accuse the wrong person, so attention to details is needed in this game. The rumour has it that if you unlock all achievements in this game and find a hidden easter egg you’ll get a job at NSA.

You probably heard the term 'Orwellian', 'Big Brother' or 'NewSpeak'. These terms come from the book Nineteen Eighty-Four (1984), a dystopian social science fiction novel by George Orwell, written in 1949 shortly after Word War II.

In this game you are monitoring citizens by listening in on their calls, watching their social media and pulling information from web sites, and by doing so gathering information. Your supervisors will then determine if they are a security risk and take action. The data you supply can be conflicting and it is left up to you to decide which data is true and thus steer your supervisors in the right (or wrong) directions. I have not finished the game, but I suspect that you will discover facts along the way that will sway you to work against your employers and have you try to help overthrow the government.

I do like they game, but I find it difficult to know what still should be done when you get stuck (aka it looks like you have nothing more to do but the game does not move forward). I have taken to the internet to watch playthroughs to get same hints of what I should do next. Some in-game hints would have been nice.

This gave me utter chills at the end because everything comes very clear. I won't spoil it but it goes to show that getting caught up in your job can be dangerous... potentially even to yourself.

There's something questionable about digging dirt on people and their lives. Watching their every move, invading their privacy. Nobody is safe, not even yourself as a govt investigator. Which will make you question your own ethics and morals. Who is really the hero in this story? Who are the true victims? Who is actually guilty and who was framed by your actions? Were you truly doing your job or were you groomed and manipulated?

It's a rather interesting ride that gathers speed and doesn't let up at the end. It makes you think that if you can incriminate someone with just a few uttered words taken out of context and twisted to another's agenda... what's preventing that from happening today?
Love the concept, but should have gone deeper.  Had it beat the first time in about 4 hours.
Nice game, the amount of choices you have to make is what makes this game sort of deep in story.

I was only intending to come back to this shortly to 100% the game, but I was very quickly reminded how excellent of an experience Orwell Season 1 is. The game has choice-based gameplay ala Telltale and Quantic Dream but is much more nuanced in its approach, allowing mostly complete freedom over what information the player decides to upload and share to this program. The story is very interesting and has a few plot twists to keep things interesting, and these are perfectly timed as well, occurring almost exactly when you think you've figured it out. Despite the game being entirely text and image based, it succeeds in being significantly more interesting than some higher budget titles which put a lot more time into their narratives. The soundtrack is also surprisingly good, and is even dynamic to an extent, changing when you read certain bits of texts that have reveals in them. It's a great time, doesn't overstay its welcome and is the perfect price, so I'd highly recommend it. 9/10.
Good story and great capture of the totalitarianism feel.

While Orwell may seem like a visual novel at the first glance, it is actually an intricate puzzle you must solve in order to unveil the truth hiding behind the datachunks.
It is hard to speak about the story of this game without giving any spoilers. That is why I can only mention that the authors try to lure you into following misleading data. But, even if you pay great attention to the details, the final chapter still has a potential to surprise you.
If you are like me and simply must have all the achievements unlocked to be satisfied, you will have to play Orwell at least thrice. But the experience isn't tedious as playing the game for the second time gives you some insight into things you might have overlooked during the initial playthrough.
In the end, this game is for the people who love games that make one think. Not just think to solve the problems and be able to finish the game. No. To think about the message of the game.
That's why I liked Orwell so much. The creators don't force their point of view on you, but rather make you think about it. There is no black and white - just two sides of the same coin.

A short game, but a thought-provoking experience.
Most of your choices have consequences. Orwell illustrates nicely how only seeing part of a story can influence one's mindset about it, or the actions that are taken in times of crisis. If you don't dig deep enough and try to get to the real crux of the matter, terrible things can happen. And they did! And honestly, on my first playthrough, I felt TERRIBLE about some of the choices I made. Quite powerful for a video game to do that.
The actual 'gameplay' is fine; repetitive, but I didn't find it boring. It might be more difficult to get through for someone who doesn't enjoy reading lots of articles, looking through the characters' profiles etc, and making some logical deductions based on the information. There's a lot of reading and not all of it relevant to the case, but all serves to flesh out the world we're supposedly living in.
My only real gripes are that a) there's just the one case. I finished the story after 4 hours or so, and the remaining playtime is just me going for achievements. It makes sense considering the ending, but I was a little sad when I realised as the concept is such a cool one! And b) no voice acting. Reading the phone calls got a bit tedious and was immersion-breaking for me.
Overall, a great and thought-provoking game with a solid concept. Would love to see it continued through multiple sequels with different stories, but the same ideas/interface/gameplay.

Here, like in many story driven games, the gameplay is just a tool to deliver the plot, and the only thing that really matters is if it does it well without being too distracting. This may be up to personal taste, but i found it enjoyable enough that i didn't feel bored at any moment. Overall would recommend it, especially if you're looking for a good engaging story.

The Orwell games are simply brilliant. No, seriously, there’s no hidden “but” here. If there ever was a series of games that I can recommend to literally everybody, it would be these two. Not because of their gameplay or their writing, though both of those are still good. No, the reason why I recommend you go out, buy and play these two games is because nothing I’ve seen elsewhere demonstrates the problems of government surveillance better than this.

In the first game, you’re put into the role of an agent tasked with finding the people responsible for a terrorist attack involving the detonation of an explosive at a public plaza. This all takes place in a fictional country called The Nation. The character you play as isn’t a citizen of The Nation though. Its government is outsourcing the surveillance of its people to external contractors who get paid to scour the internet and tap into phone conversations. Your job is to feed information back to a software called Orwell, which stores and processes all this data. You also have an advisor, who only gets to see the data that you feed into the software and they draw their own conclusions based on what information you feed them, which also determine certain future actions in the narrative. You can choose to omit information and sometimes you find conflicting or contradictory information where you have to choose, which of the two you want to pass along, since it doesn’t allow you to just collect both.

You get to violate the privacy of a number of citizens of the Nation and in the process have to figure out who’s behind the attacks. Naturally, everybody has a motive, since the government of the Nation isn’t too well regarded in certain spheres of its population. 

What fascinates me the most here is that both games obviously want to steer you into doing the right thing. And by “the right thing”, I mean to not simply rat out everybody and instead really take in the context of what people are saying. Every data chunk that you can collect in your database tells you what exactly is being extracted from it. So, if, say, a character is angry and says something metaphorically threatening or violent or if someone is generally impulsive, the data chunk reveals that Orwell and your advisor always take stuff like this 100% literally. There’s no room for nuanced interpretation or metaphor. It really makes you consider what information you’re willing to feed into the system and what’s better left where it is.

At first, I thought that this was fairly annoying, especially because it can also happen at times when you really have no other choice than to pick up that data chunk for the story to progress. But that too is part of the message that the game is sending. Government surveillance often lacks context and instead uses isolated details from which to conclude the bigger picture. Multiple times, your advisor draws conclusions and puts actions into motion against characters just as new information about them is coming to light, so the game constantly reminds you that these are supposed to be real people. They may lie to certain characters too and therefore lead you into the wrong direction. And forcing you to ignore that context at certain points even though you’re aware that it exists should tell you as a player something about government surveillance and maybe inform your opinion of it. The game also forces you to focus only on characters that the game lets you investigate. Now this is obviously a limitation of the game in and of itself because the developers can’t create tons of meaningless characters for you to investigate only for the lead to go nowhere. But it also once again comments on how government surveillance can sometimes turn a blind eye to the obvious by merely focusing on whatever is directly in front of it. 

The thing is though that at this point I have to mention that the actual gameplay is fairly simplistic and rudimentary. In essence it’s little more than a visual novel, since most of the time you’re just reading. There’s little in terms of flair going on, you’re literally just staring at a piece of software for most of it, browsing the web or reading along with phone calls and text messages. The second game thankfully features some voice acting for the phone conversations and podcasts, but you’re still mostly just reading stuff. I get that this isn’t everybody’s cup of tea and that many people don’t play games to simply sit there and read something, so the Orwell games won’t be for everybody. But I’d still urge you to try them out simply because of how effectively they convey their message. They’re also not that long, the first game takes around 5 hours to complete. Though there’s plenty of replay value to see how things might turn out otherwise if you made other decisions and maybe played as a blindly loyal character who doesn’t care whose lives he gets to ruin. So yeah, all in all, I definitely recommend the Orwell games.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive dystopian mystery clicker with one of the most obvious titles on this planet. Seriously, tell me you don't have an inkling of what this game is about just by reading it. No? 
Well - Orwell touches on government surveillance, privacy in the age of send/receive, newsfeeds and - on the philosophical level - shockingly personal themes such as morality, autonomy and group culture. It also teeters on the sociological side of things with themes of the looking-glass self, or how we present ourselves to the world/others. Let's talk about the narrative. I'll try not to spoil too much.

------------------------------------

You are, well, yourself. You live in a non-disclosed location as an investigator who has just been contracted to work on a secret government project by The Nation; A country that is, simply put, not doing so great from the leadership aspect. The Nation is undergoing political turmoil, both inner and outer, and is seeing a concerning increase in violence, extremism and terrorist attacks. This has led the country to establish increasingly dystopian methods of surveillance. 

The beginning scene sets the tone with you looking through multiple sets of cameras on an otherwise normal day in a city square. The cameras scan the citizens, seemingly referencing police files to determine if they're a threat. So far, so good! A blue haired girl quietly walks past and the camera begins to buzz, showing that - !!! - she has had an encounter with the law in the past. We tensely follow her as she gets on a bus and it drives away. Hm. Well, surely that's not THAT out of the ordinary, right? We all know someone who has a blot on their record. Surely, we shouldn't judge unless they've done something terrible? I'll reserve my judgement. 

And then a statue a short distance away is engulfed in dust, shrapnel and the sounds of an otherwise normal day being eviscerated as a bomb explodes. Well, damn.

This is where you come in, Investigator. You have been hired to test the efficacy of the brand new "Orwell" project. Orwell is a hot-off-the-assembly-line database tool that allows you to search nearly anything there is to know about a person. It creates links between people for referencing and logs any interesting findings you catch - referred to as 'datachunks' within each person's "file". Your job is to prevent any other terrorist attacks from occurring as well as finding out who could've been behind such a horrible event.

-------------------------------------

The success of Orwell is predicated on it's atmosphere - and it is indeed the game's biggest asset. However...

If I can be quite honest - the writing itself isn't anything revolutionary here when it comes to it's subject matter. Some of the dialogue is great, engrossing even. Some of it is extraordinarily cringey, for lack of a better word. A certain aforementioned blue-haired character comes to mind, especially near the end game. Some laughably unbelievable behavior occurs that can really mess with your vibe once you understand exactly how the plot is shaping itself.

Writing quibbles aside, immersion is ultimately what reigns supreme here. The developers have created such an oppressively paranoid atmosphere with the simple interface and nerve-wracking audio cues that it's incredibly easy to be charmed and overlook it's relatively short length. This is a game that benefits from not overstepping it's own ambition. 

I've seen a few other reviews being slightly critical of the fact that more characters weren't involved in the overall game - but I think that this actually works in Orwell's favor. The gameplay is the *absolute* definition of repetitive. You shift between tabs, you drag and you drop. That's it. If the gameplay wasn't so story centric and was more sim-based (with more options within the Orwell interface), I would agree with those criticisms and want to be Big Brother until the end of time. However, this is an actual story game. Consider this to be a dystopian choose your own adventure.

To end this ramble, let's talk length and price. I spent 3.4 hours on this game and completed it. It's currently $9.99 on Steam. I myself, being transparent, did not pay $9.99 for this. I received it in a bundle along with it's sequel. So you ultimately will have to make your own call here - but I will say that YES - Orwell is indeed worth $10 just for the first playthrough alone. 

Not very many games touch upon these themes, and I do consider these to be important themes considering the time/political climate we live in right now. Regardless of how successful the game is at making a statement on these themes, I appreciate the effort. And a lot of effort has gone into this game. 

I very much recommend you give it the chance, it may very well cause you to look over both digital shoulders.

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a great game that really embraces the Orwellian themes around government surveillance and intrusion of privacy. Having had to study George Orwell's novels in school, I can say for sure that the immersion of stepping into the world of the texts is definitely present. Having both elements of seriousness in maintaining the peace and order of the nation, coupled with a few occasionally humorous moments helped to offset the tiresome feeling of focusing too hard on the 'job' and rather reminds us to realise that the system is in fact still inept at reading human communications. This draws into my next point in that initially, I thought that the game would be a lot more general with more cases, similar to quantity over quality. However, I soon realised that having the player focus on one specific case was much better, in fact, as there was a lot more pressure on you to suffer the consequences of having ingrained human qualities pertaining morality and such. Overall, it's a brilliant game, albeit a rather short one, that allows for a few more playthroughs after the initial run.

The beginning of the "game" starts off in a typical direction where you use the power of the state to spy on these fictional characters, I felt disgusted as spying on people in general I consider to be morally reprehensible. Due to this, my first play-through was played in such a way to make progress for the state as difficult as I possibly can, it is quite an achievement that the game actually gives you the option to do this, to its credit. However, that is when issues on game progression started occurring, I would expect that it would be quite easy to proceed through the game if you started dragging and dropping everything highlighted in blue or yellow into the profiler, but if you wanted to play as a rebel then you will quite easily get stuck. 

Let me explain, to play under a persona of liberty you need to omit certain details from the system, but some of these details must be recorded to progress in the game even though associating a character with the data is against your play-through persona. This actually leads to a lot of frustration due to being "stuck" because you refuse to drag/drop a very specific keyword or phrase to advance the game, or if you somehow missed it and have to dig through all the content all over again.

There are some good points about this indoctrination drag/drop simulator.
The universe that was created including the text content, phone calls, chats and character profiles have quite a bit of effort put into them making a somewhat cohesive story.

If you've ever read any dystopic novels and enjoyed them (not just 1984, but Brave New World, Fahrenheit 451 etc.) then this is a very fun game to enter such a world. However the perspective change with Orwell is that you become the one controlling the panopticon, and your choices determine who gets arrested and killed, what big events happen in the game, and what ultimately happens to this program that allows 'foreigners' to spy on people of 'The Nation' (the fictional country the game is set in). 

This is also quite a nice game to play if you don't feel up to quick or intense action you find in others. This game, if you want to delve deep into the world, contains a lot of reading and clicking/dragging highlighted bits of text. That's about it. And you can enjoy 5-8 hours of this, which is especially good if you get this game very cheaply when it comes on sale. The story is engaging and has very interesting characters. I have not played the sequel, but reviews on it say that it's not as good as the first Orwell game (this one). 

Pros: 
- very good soundtrack
- good story, but has little replayability considering you already know the truth of what happens later, and the consequences of your choices
- you can replay individual chapters when you go to "Profile Options" after completing the game on a profile, which means it is very easy to achievement hunt (which is what I did)
- good length of the game, even if it's not on sale
- unique mechanics I haven't played in a game before (I don't play all that many indies however)

Cons:
- the story replayability aspect
- if you're not very interested in 1984 or Orwell's writings then this may not interest you all that much considering that this game is one big reference to 1984

I recommend this one at a sale price.  A complete playthrough took me about 5 1/2 hours.  If you check out lets play videos before buying I would caution you not to watch too much beyond seeing the game mechanics as you don't want to spoil the story.

You play the role of an investigator, basically a detective in a world where you have access to people's phones & computers and can eavesdrop on your targets' communications to try to thwart terrorism.  You choose which information to pass on to the government that hired you and they in turn use that information to make law enforcement decisions.

I've only played one time, but I get the idea that the story can change depending on which pieces of information you decide to pass along.  It's not a wide open world with different cases, so I don't find replayability here.  It plays more like a novel where you play the role of one of the characters, and it does this very well.  Lots of reading snippets of information and conversations - not linear like actually reading a book, but linear in that the story is already there and you're discovering it.

Sadly, you can only play it for the first time once.  Like a good book I think this will be one of those games that I'll play again in a couple years after I've forgotten a lot of it so that I can enjoy it again in a fresh way.  Recommended for 5-6 hours of play, or more if you like going back and seeing what different choices do.

Orwell to my comprehension is a game set in Britain, being in a timeline where camera's and invasive technology are being ushered in by the government, under the guise of safety. The game's premise, location and the name itself draw distinct premise to a book, written by an individual who fought the Spaniards in the 20th century. The man had other notable accomplishments, such as wrestling adult elephants in front of rural Indian villagers, as a gesture of the might of Great Britian. In essence, it is inherently blatant that this idea being presented in Orwell is exceptionally intriguing, however, it all turns awry. 

What I have had to endure is worse than potential intrusion and subsequent sexual depravity at the government, Orwell is none other than a point and click adventure game. Woe and despair have betided me, for In the history of fabled lore, no successful game has abided by a point and click adventure structure, it is inherently a recipe for disaster, one that only lunatics and fiends will attempt to pursue. However, due to my own altruistic merit, I attempted engage and judge Orwell in an impartial way, albeit I remained wary. Within time, it became clear that my fears were correct. In a game of this calibre dialogue or the development of the ambience becomes imperative, however, unfortunately this game was the opposite. On numerous occasions I encountered various fallacies in Orwell's writing, for example they stated "Mom" as opposed to the genuine spelling in Britain, that is "Mum". Alongside this trivial mistake, the rest of the dialogue is utterly obsolete, with the intel being utterly repetitive and tedious, having no distinctive effect on the genuine flow of the game. This affirms my belief that the armies of Tartarus have escaped their confinement and harnassed the power of the internet, attempting to conduct a period of psychological warfare upon their adversaries, which just so happen to be the denizens of Steam. Likely, you are currently contemplating that I am exaggerating, being prone to drama or embellishment, in preparation of this event I summarised a portion of the dialogue, certifying my analysis. The first individual stated, "Hey can you bomb this square for me?", with the other responding, "I don't want to commit a terrorist attack". This statement was then countered by the resolute, "Awww, I baked muffins.", following by the individual relenting and going, "Bah, you discovered my weakness, fine ill do it." It is a rare circumstance that I feel the necessity to go on a blood curling massacre, reaping havoc upon the local populace, however, after witnessing this peculiar exchange in game I allowed myself the luxury. It is completely baffling how an innocuous, benign statement regarding muffins can be used to convince an individual into committing a terrorist attack, the writers have had their minds completely distorted of all forms of sanity, leaving an unhinged, muffin crazed remnant of a mind to remain. The ludicrousness of the writing then conveniently places an entrance into the other main gripe, the character interactions. The characters continuously, throughout the game converse in the most inhuman fashion I have ever encountered, every attempt at conversation is filled to the brim with various Emoji's, faces concocted out of text and abbreviations that produce an incoherent spiralled mess. This then raises complications, as some of the characters are supposed professional writers, working for reputable news company. This conflicts with their genuine writing style however, which appears filled to the brim with profanity, grammatical errors and a blatant attempt at attempting to mimic the stereotypical view that I assume millennial's believe, regarding today's youth. While I can completely comprehend the fact that the writers are likely forced to induce semen daily, tortured after falling asleep on their 20 hour shift and are likely in solitude, away from any form of sentient life away from the workplace, it still bears no excuse to the shoddily, artificial dialogue. On a game so reliant on literature and character interaction, it falls abruptly into an expertly crafted brick wall. I have engaged in many endeavour's throughout my time and out of every calamity I have endured, Orwell by far contains the most infuriating dialogue. These character's are blatantly not from this planet, as they type in an utterly erratic and volatile fashion, which complete with the apparent subtle clues leading to unique plot twists, causes a smouldering mess. I enjoyed Orwell, and I think it's worth playing through at least once, but I don't think the social commentary is particularly sharp.

The surveillance system that it depicts is set up in an incredibly obtuse manner. You can sometimes accept a misinterpreted piece of data as the truth (like accepting that a target "engages in torture" when a childhood friend mentions that they playfully "tortured" her), and sometimes you have to pick between conflicting pieces of data without having sufficient context for deciding yet. This is all in the context of a "safety bill" that allows people to be prosecuted for the implication of a crime, rather than an actual crime.

That you can set up a really poor surveillance system in a state that already has a law that violates basic principles of justice, is not particularly good criticism of the idea of a surveillance state. Far better points could have been made in a game in the post-Snowden era, given the extent of the actual surveillance revealed.

Still, any game that makes people think about a surveillance state, and whether they want to continue living in one can only be good.
